title: Berkshire 2012 letter: float, buybacks, dividends vs sell-off, and staying in the game
summary: Buffett reviews 2012 and explains why Berkshire measures itself on intrinsic value against the S&P. He covers insurance float as a revolving fund, price discipline in buybacks, why a sell-off policy beats dividends, and why timing the market is a mistake. He also admits capital-allocation errors.

principles.text: Judge management by growth in intrinsic value versus the S&P; otherwise investors should just buy a low-cost index fund.
principles.quote: It’s our job to increase intrinsic business value – for which we use book value as a significantly understated proxy – at a faster rate than the market gains of the S&P.

principles.text: Don't dance in and out of stocks on forecasts; the risks of being out of the game exceed the risks of being in it.
principles.quote: Charlie and I believe it’s a terrible mistake to try to dance in and out of it based upon the turn of tarot cards, the predictions of “experts,” or the ebb and flow of business activity.

principles.text: Good insurance requires walking away when the right premium can't be had; copying competitors' pricing spells trouble.
principles.quote: Many insurers pass the first three tests and flunk the fourth. They simply can’t turn their back on business that is being eagerly written by their competitors.

principles.text: Float is a revolving fund; if it is costless and long-enduring, its true liability value is far below the accounting figure.
principles.quote: If float is both costless and long-enduring, which I believe Berkshire’s will be, the true value of this liability is dramatically less than the accounting liability.

principles.text: Repurchase only when shares trade at a meaningful discount to intrinsic value; paying above it destroys value.
principles.quote: But never forget: In repurchase decisions, price is all-important. Value is destroyed when purchases are made above intrinsic value.

principles.text: Prefer a wonderful business at a fair price to a fair business at a wonderful price; bargain-hunting habits cause mistakes.
principles.quote: More than 50 years ago, Charlie told me that it was far better to buy a wonderful business at a fair price than to buy a fair business at a wonderful price.
